title: Teaching and Learning
description: Class 19 practice: the domains of learning, readiness to learn, planning teaching, teach-back and evaluation, teaching across the lifespan, and learning theories and the nurse's role in client education, matched to the professor's Exam 4 blueprint.

discharge.intro: A nurse on a medical unit is preparing a client for discharge tomorrow.

tabs.title: Nurse's Notes
tabs.html:
Nurse's Notes

Day 3, 0900: 72-year-old client admitted with new type 2 diabetes; now prescribed basal insulin by pen once daily. Lives alone; daughter visits weekly. Wears glasses, which are at the bedside. Says, “I left school in eighth grade.” Slept poorly because of a noisy roommate; yawning and asks to rest. Blood glucose 168 mg/dL. Denies pain.

1400: Awake after a 2-hour nap and alert. Picks up the insulin pen from the tray and asks to hold it. Says, “I want to learn to do the shot so I can take care of myself.”

tabs.title: Teaching Plan
tabs.html:
Teaching Plan: insulin pen

By discharge, the client will:

  1. Prime the pen with 2 units and dial the prescribed dose.
  2. Inject into the abdomen and hold the needle in place for 10 seconds.
  3. Explain, in his own words, the signs of low blood glucose and what to do.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning teaching for a client who has a new colostomy. Which learning objective belongs in the psychomotor domain?
options: The client will describe the signs of a blocked stoma by day 3.
The client will empty and rinse the pouch without help by day 3.
The client will share feelings about the change in body image by day 3.
The client will list foods that commonly cause gas by day 3.
questions.rationale:
The psychomotor domain is the "skill" domain: doing something with the hands and body. Emptying and rinsing the pouch is a skill the nurse can watch the client perform.

Describing the signs of a blocked stoma isn't the right answer. It's about the stoma and sounds practical, but describing is thinking: the cognitive domain. Listing foods is cognitive too. Sharing feelings about body image belongs to the affective ("feeling") domain.

Takeaway: Cognitive is thinking (describe, list, explain), affective is feeling (accept, value, share feelings), and psychomotor is doing (a skill you can watch).

questions.stem: A nurse has finished teaching a client how to use a metered-dose inhaler with a spacer. Which method should the nurse use to evaluate this learning?
options: Ask the client to explain each step of using the inhaler
Give the client a short written quiz on the spacer steps
Ask how confident she feels with the inhaler and spacer
Watch the client use the inhaler and spacer
questions.rationale:
Using an inhaler with a spacer is a psychomotor skill, so the best evidence of learning is a return demonstration: the nurse watches the client do it and corrects the technique.

Explaining each step isn't the right answer: teach-back is so common, but a client can recite the steps and still hold the inhaler wrong or breathe in too fast. Teach-back checks understanding (cognitive); a skill needs to be seen. A written quiz also checks only knowledge, and how confident she feels is self-report, which can't show whether the technique is correct.

Takeaway: Match the evaluation to the domain: a skill is evaluated by watching it (return demonstration); knowledge by teach-back, questions, or a test.

questions.stem: A client newly diagnosed with type 2 diabetes correctly explains his meal plan and names the carbohydrate foods in it. He then says, “I'm not going to be one of those people who can't have cake at a party. Diets are for sick people.” Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Explore what this diagnosis means to the client
Review the meal plan again with a new handout
Have the client plan a full day of meals on paper
Document that the teaching outcome was met
questions.rationale:
The client has shown cognitive learning (he can explain the plan), but his statement shows he hasn't accepted the diagnosis or valued the change: affective learning hasn't happened. The nurse addresses it by exploring what the diagnosis means to him, his feelings and beliefs, before expecting the behavior to change.

Documenting that the outcome was met isn't the right answer, even though he passed the knowledge check. But confirmed cognitive learning doesn't ensure affective learning, and he has just said he won't follow the plan. Reviewing the plan again and planning a day of meals both repeat cognitive teaching he has already mastered.

Takeaway: Knowing isn't accepting. When a client can explain the plan but rejects it, teach to the affective domain: explore feelings, beliefs, and values.

questions.stem: A nurse is writing affective-domain objectives for a client recovering from a myocardial infarction. Which objectives should the nurse include?
options: The client expresses feelings about returning to work.
The client states that quitting smoking is worth the effort.
The client takes his own radial pulse for one full minute.
The client lists three warning signs of a heart attack.
The client chooses to join a cardiac rehabilitation support group.
The client explains how nitroglycerin relieves chest pain.
questions.rationale:
The affective domain covers feelings, attitudes, and values. Expressing feelings about returning to work, stating that quitting is worth it (valuing a change), and choosing to join a support group (acting on a value) are all affective.

Explaining how nitroglycerin works isn't the right answer: it's about the client's own treatment and sounds personal, but explaining is cognitive, as is listing warning signs. Taking a radial pulse is a skill: psychomotor.

Takeaway: Look at the verb: express, value, choose, and accept are affective; list and explain are cognitive; perform and demonstrate are psychomotor.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching the parent of an infant how to give a liquid medication with an oral syringe. Which teaching strategy should the nurse use?
options: Give a printed sheet with a picture of each step
Discuss each step with the parent, then answer any questions
Demonstrate it, then have the parent practice giving a dose
Show a short video on giving oral medications
questions.rationale:
Measuring and giving a dose with a syringe is a psychomotor skill, and psychomotor skills need practice: discussion alone isn't enough. The nurse demonstrates, then has the parent practice, correcting as needed.

Discussing the steps and answering questions isn't the right answer: it's interactive and invites questions, but the parent never handles the syringe. A picture sheet and a video are useful supports that use the eyes, but neither gives practice.

Takeaway: Skills are learned by doing: demonstrate, then have the learner practice until performance is correct.

questions.stem: A nurse's teaching plan for a client starting warfarin has three objectives: the client will explain why to keep vitamin K intake steady, will brush with a soft toothbrush, and will accept the need for regular blood tests. Which evaluation method matches the first objective?
options: Watch the client brush his teeth with the soft toothbrush
Ask the client how he feels about regular blood tests
Have him tell, in his own words, why leafy greens matter
Check the client's INR result at the next clinic visit
questions.rationale:
The first objective is cognitive: the client will explain a reason. The matching evaluation is to ask him to explain it in his own words.

Checking the INR isn't the right answer, even though it's objective data and a stable INR is the goal of the teaching. But many things change an INR, and a lab result doesn't show whether the client understands vitamin K. Watching him brush evaluates the second (psychomotor) objective, and asking how he feels about blood tests evaluates the third (affective) one.

Takeaway: Each objective's verb names its evaluation: explain is checked by asking, perform by watching, and accept by listening for feelings and values.

questions.stem: A nurse taught a client with a new ileostomy how to care for it. Which observations should the nurse document as evidence that learning occurred?
options: Changes the pouch correctly while the nurse watches
Describes, in his own words, when to call the provider
Nods and says “that makes sense” after each step
Signs the form stating that teaching was received
Watched the full ostomy care video in his room
Empties the pouch on his own when it is one-third full
questions.rationale:
Evidence of learning is a change in behavior that can be observed and measured. Changing the pouch correctly (return demonstration), describing when to call in his own words (teach-back), and emptying the pouch on his own at the right time are all behaviors the nurse can see.

Nodding and saying "that makes sense" isn't the right answer. It sounds like understanding, but agreement isn't evidence: clients often nod to be polite. Signing a form shows teaching was given, not learned, and watching a video is exposure to information, not proof of learning.

Takeaway: Document what the client did or said in his own words, not that he agreed, signed, or watched.

questions.stem: A client recovering from a stroke must learn to walk with a quad cane before discharge. Which outcome statement should the nurse write for this teaching?
options: Walks 50 feet with the quad cane, using the correct sequence, by discharge
Understands how to use the quad cane safely and correctly by discharge
Watches the physical therapist walk with the quad cane by discharge
Feels confident about walking with the quad cane at home by discharge
questions.rationale:
A learning outcome names a behavior the learner will perform that can be observed and measured, with a time frame. Walking 50 feet with the correct sequence can be watched and checked, and it fits the skill being taught.

Understands how to use the cane isn't the right answer: understanding sounds like learning, but "understands" can't be observed or measured. Watching the therapist describes something the client sees, not something the client does. Feeling confident is affective and matters, but it doesn't show the skill was learned.

Takeaway: Write outcomes with an action verb you can observe (walks, demonstrates, states), a measure, and a time frame; avoid "understands" and "knows".

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a client with newly diagnosed hypertension about a low-sodium diet. Which statement by the client shows learning in the affective domain?
options: “I should keep my sodium under the limit I was given.”
“I can find the sodium on a food label in the store.”
“High sodium makes my body hold on to extra fluid.”
“I've decided my health is worth cutting back on salt.”
questions.rationale:
Affective learning is a change in attitudes and values. Saying that her health is worth cutting back on salt shows she values the change.

Keeping sodium under the limit isn't the right answer. It sounds committed, but it restates a rule she was taught: cognitive. Explaining that sodium holds fluid is also cognitive. Finding sodium on a label is a skill she can show in the store.

Takeaway: Affective statements reveal what the client values or has decided ("worth it", "I've decided"); cognitive statements repeat facts or rules.

questions.stem: A nurse plans to teach a client, 1 day after a hip replacement, how to use a walker. The client is grimacing, rates pain 8 on a scale of 0 to 10, and asks, “Can we do this later?” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Begin teaching, keeping the session short and simple
Give the prescribed pain medication, then return to teach
Leave a handout on walker safety for the client to read
Ask the physical therapist to teach the walker instead
questions.rationale:
Pain is a physiologic factor that blocks learning, and physical needs come before teaching (Maslow). The nurse treats the pain first, then teaches when the client can focus and move.

A short, simple session isn't the right answer: keeping it brief sounds considerate, but a client in severe pain can't learn a new skill, however short the lesson. A handout doesn't relieve the pain and can't teach a skill that needs practice. The physical therapist would face the same pain.

Takeaway: Pain, fatigue, and strong emotions block learning. Meet the physical need first, then teach.

questions.stem: A nurse is assessing whether a client with newly diagnosed diabetes is ready to learn about insulin. Which findings suggest readiness?
options: Asks how the insulin will fit with her work schedule
Changes the subject whenever the diagnosis comes up
Picks up the insulin pen on the tray and asks to hold it
Keeps the television on while the nurse is explaining
Has canceled two diabetes education appointments
Says she wants to be able to take care of herself at home
questions.rationale:
A client who is ready to learn asks questions (how insulin fits her work), shows interest (asks to hold the pen), and recognizes the learning need (wants to care for herself).

Keeping the television on may look harmless, but it shows inattention, a cue that she isn't ready. Changing the subject suggests she hasn't accepted the diagnosis, and canceling appointments is a classic sign of low motivation.

Takeaway: Ready learners ask questions, reach for the equipment, and name their own goals; minimal interest, inattention, and canceled appointments signal low readiness.

questions.stem: A client learned of a cancer diagnosis an hour ago and is crying. The nurse has wound care teaching scheduled before the client's discharge this afternoon. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Sit with the client and encourage her to talk about the news
Teach the wound care now, since discharge is set for today
Give the written wound care instructions and offer to answer questions
Teach the wound care to the client's husband while she rests
questions.rationale:
Strong emotions such as fear, grief, and anxiety inhibit learning. The client can't take in wound care right now, so the nurse first responds to her emotional state, then teaches when she's able to focus.

Teaching her husband isn't the right answer, even though involving a support person is often wise, and he can help at home. But it bypasses the client, who is the learner, and leaves her distress unaddressed. Teaching now ignores the emotional barrier, and written instructions handed to a crying client won't be read or understood.

Takeaway: Address strong emotions before teaching; learning can't happen until the client can focus.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse, “I never finished school, and I don't read much.” Which teaching material should the nurse choose for this client?
options: A detailed handout written at a high school level
A large-print booklet with each medical term defined
A short video with pictures that shows each step
A website the client can read at home later
questions.rationale:
Clients with minimal literacy need information presented through audio or visuals. A short video with pictures teaches without depending on reading.

A large-print booklet with terms defined isn't the right answer: it seems to make reading easier, but large print helps vision, not reading ability, and definitions add more words. A high school-level handout and a website both depend on reading.

Takeaway: For low literacy, use pictures, audio, video, demonstration, and plain spoken language; don't just make the print bigger.

questions.stem: Over three visits, a client says he forgot his reading glasses each time the nurse hands him printed material, and he asks his wife to fill out his forms. He follows spoken directions well. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Give the client large-print handouts at the next visit
Assess the client's literacy in a private, respectful way
Teach the wife, since she manages the paperwork at home
Refer the client to an eye care provider for a vision exam
questions.rationale:
Repeated excuses ("forgot my glasses"), asking others to complete forms, and doing well with spoken directions are common cues of low literacy. The nurse assesses reading ability privately and respectfully, so the teaching plan can fit the client without shaming him.

A vision exam isn't the right answer: the client blames his glasses, but he follows spoken directions well and the pattern points to reading, not seeing. Large print rests on the same wrong assumption. Teaching the wife leaves out the client, who is the learner.

Takeaway: Excuses to avoid reading and relying on others for forms suggest low literacy: assess it privately, then teach with spoken words, pictures, and demonstration.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning when and where to teach a client how to change a dressing. Which choice best supports learning?
options: Right after the client's physical therapy session
At the bedside while the roommate has visitors
Just before discharge, so the steps are fresh
After the client's nap, in a quiet room
questions.rationale:
Timing and environment are factors that help learning. After a nap, in a quiet room, the client is rested and free of distractions.

Just before discharge isn't the right answer: the steps would be fresh, but last-minute teaching leaves no time for practice, questions, or reteaching. Right after physical therapy the client is likely tired, and a roommate's visitors distract.

Takeaway: Teach when the client is rested and comfortable, in a quiet place, with enough time to practice before discharge.

questions.stem: A client with type 2 diabetes shows little interest in teaching about diet, but lights up when he talks about playing soccer with his grandchildren. Which approach is most likely to motivate the client?
options: Explain the long-term complications of uncontrolled diabetes
Give him a detailed meal plan with exact portions to follow
Tell him the provider expects his A1C to improve by next visit
Link the diet changes to staying active with his family
questions.rationale:
One of the best ways to raise motivation is to relate the learning to something the client values. Connecting the diet to staying active with his family, like playing soccer with his grandchildren, gives him a reason that matters to him.

Explaining long-term complications isn't the right answer: the facts are true and serious, but fear of distant problems rarely motivates someone who isn't engaged. A detailed meal plan adds content before he's interested, and the provider's expectation is someone else's goal, not his.

Takeaway: Motivation grows when teaching connects to what the client values; find it, then build the teaching around it.

questions.stem: A client with hypertension hasn't been taking her prescribed medication, and a coworker calls her “noncompliant.” Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Reteach the purpose of the medication and its schedule
Ask what makes the daily doses hard for her
Document the client's nonadherence in the medical record
Ask the provider about switching to a once-daily medication
questions.rationale:
Before labeling a client noncompliant, the nurse finds out why she isn't following the plan: cost, side effects, confusion, beliefs, or access. Asking what has made it hard is the assessment that guides everything else.

Reteaching isn't the right answer: a learning need seems likely, but it assumes the reason is lack of knowledge, and she may understand perfectly and be unable to afford the drug. Switching medications is a solution before the problem is known, and documenting nonadherence applies the label the nurse should hold off on.

Takeaway: Don't label a client noncompliant until you know why; assess the reason first, then plan teaching or other help.

questions.stem: A nurse is asked to teach a client how to use a newly prescribed insulin pen. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Write learning objectives for the insulin pen session
Choose a video that shows how to use the insulin pen
Find out what the client already knows about insulin
Demonstrate the pen using a practice injection pad
questions.rationale:
Teaching follows the nursing process, and the first step is assessment: what the client already knows, whether he can learn, his readiness, and how he prefers to learn. Every later step depends on it.

Writing objectives isn't the right answer: planning comes early, but objectives can't be set before the nurse knows what the client needs. Choosing a video and demonstrating are implementation steps that come later.

Takeaway: The first step in teaching is assessing the learner: background knowledge, ability, readiness, and preferences.

questions.stem: A client with newly diagnosed heart failure has several learning needs before discharge. Which approach should the nurse use to set the order of teaching?
options: Decide on the priorities together with the client
Start with the topic the provider listed first in the orders
Follow the order of topics on the unit's standard care plan
Start with the topic the nurse considers the most complex
questions.rationale:
Teaching priorities are best set by the nurse and the client together. When the client's own priorities are addressed, the client is more motivated to keep going with the remaining learning needs.

Following the standard care plan isn't the right answer: it's organized and evidence-based, but it isn't tailored to this client and leaves the client out of the decision. The provider's order and the nurse's sense of complexity also skip the client's participation.

Takeaway: Involve the client in every step of planning, including the order of topics; it raises motivation.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client with heart failure about self-care at home. Which statement by the nurse uses language best suited to client teaching?
options: “Monitor for edema and report any dyspnea on exertion to your provider.”
“Weigh yourself each morning after you use the bathroom, before you eat.”
“Restrict fluids to 1,500 mL per day, and keep a record of your I&O.”
“Watch for signs of fluid volume excess, such as rapid weight gain.”
questions.rationale:
When teaching, the nurse communicates clearly and concisely, in a layperson's vocabulary. "Weigh yourself each morning after you use the bathroom, before you eat" uses everyday words and tells the client exactly what to do.

"Watch for signs of fluid volume excess" isn't the right answer: it gives an example the client can recognize, but "fluid volume excess" is nursing language. Edema and dyspnea on exertion are medical terms, and mL and I&O are abbreviations a client may not know.

Takeaway: Teach in plain words the client uses every day, and say exactly what to do; translate medical terms and abbreviations.

questions.stem: A client with newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes drinks six cans of regular soda a day. The nurse and the client are setting a goal. Which goal is best?
options: The client will stop drinking regular soda starting today.
The client will understand how soda raises blood glucose.
The client will drink less regular soda over the next few months.
The client will swap three daily sodas for water within 2 weeks.
questions.rationale:
The behavior change expected from teaching must be realistic, and a goal must be measurable and time-bound. Replacing three sodas with water within 2 weeks is a specific, achievable first step.

Stopping all soda today isn't the right answer: it's the healthiest goal, but quitting a six-a-day habit at once is unrealistic and sets the client up to fail. Understanding how soda raises glucose can't be measured, and drinking less over the next months has no amount and no clear deadline.

Takeaway: Good goals are realistic, measurable, and time-bound; a reachable first step beats an ideal the client can't meet.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning how to teach a client to care for a new tracheostomy at home. Which plan best supports learning?
options: Start with cleaning the outer area, then add steps over several sessions
Cover the whole procedure in one session so the client sees the full process
Teach the hardest step first, while the client is most alert and rested
Give the full procedure in writing, and review it on the day of discharge
questions.rationale:
Learning is helped when information moves from simple to complex and key points are repeated. Starting with a simple part and adding steps over several sessions builds the skill and gives practice each time.

Teaching the hardest step first isn't the right answer: the client's alertness matters, but starting with the hardest part breaks the simple-to-complex rule and can discourage the client. Every step in one session overloads the learner, and written steps reviewed on discharge day leave no time to practice.

Takeaway: Build from simple to complex, spread a skill over several sessions, and repeat key steps.

questions.stem: A nurse is reviewing the unit's handout on inhaler use before teaching a 70-year-old client whose primary language is Spanish. Which findings mean the handout shouldn't be used as it is?
options: It is printed only in English.
It shows an inhaler model the unit no longer stocks.
It uses large print and simple drawings.
It was last updated eleven years ago.
It covers the steps in the client's plan of care.
It was written by the respiratory therapy department.
questions.rationale:
Teaching content must be accurate, current, consistent with the care the client gets, and adjusted for the learner's age, culture, and ability. A handout only in English isn't adjusted for this client, one showing an inhaler she won't use isn't consistent, and one eleven years old may not be current.

Written by respiratory therapy isn't a problem: it wasn't written by nursing, but a reliable, expert source is a strength. Large print and simple drawings suit an older adult, and covering the plan-of-care steps means it matches the learning outcomes.

Takeaway: Before using teaching material, check that it's accurate, current, consistent with the client's care, and fitted to the client's age, language, and abilities.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a teaching plan for a client who has a new ileostomy. Which action is most likely to increase the client's motivation to follow the plan?
options: Give the client a copy of the finished plan to keep
Ask the wound care nurse to explain the plan to the client
Involve the client in each step of making the plan
Show the client the plan the unit uses for ostomy clients
questions.rationale:
A teaching plan is best made with the client's participation, which raises the client's motivation. Involving the client in each step makes it the client's plan, not the nurse's.

Asking the wound care nurse to explain it isn't the right answer: a specialist adds expertise, but explaining a finished plan still leaves the client out of making it. A copy to keep and the unit's standard plan are handed to the client rather than built with the client.

Takeaway: Clients follow plans they helped make: involve the client in setting goals, priorities, and methods.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning to teach a client how to check her own blood glucose. Which plan best follows the principles of effective teaching?
options: Explain the steps clearly, and give her a written list of them
Have her watch a video, then answer her questions about it
Show the steps, have her practice, and give her a picture guide
Explain the steps twice, then ask if she has any questions
questions.rationale:
Teaching that uses more than one sense enhances learning, and psychomotor skills need practice. Showing, practicing, and a picture guide combine seeing, doing, and a reminder for home.

Explaining the steps twice isn't the right answer: repetition does reinforce learning, but it's still only hearing, with no practice of the skill. A written list and a video with questions add a sense but still skip hands-on practice.

Takeaway: Combine senses (see, hear, do), and always include practice when teaching a skill.

questions.stem: A nurse has explained a new medication schedule to a client. Which statement by the nurse best confirms the client's understanding?
options: “To be sure I was clear, tell me how you'll take this at home.”
“Do you understand how you'll take this medication at home?”
“Show me how you'll set up your pill box for the coming week.”
“Do you have any questions about how you'll take this at home?”
questions.rationale:
The teach-back method asks the client to describe the main points in the client's own words. Framing it as checking the nurse's explanation keeps it from feeling like a test.

"Show me how you'll set up your pill box" isn't the right answer: it asks for action, but it's a return demonstration of a different skill, and it doesn't show the client knows the schedule's reasons and timing. "Do you understand?" and "Any questions?" invite a simple yes or no, which many clients answer politely without understanding.

Takeaway: Teach-back asks the client to explain in their own words; avoid yes-or-no checks like "Do you understand?"

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client about a newly prescribed diuretic and pauses for teach-back. The client says, “I'll take it at bedtime so it can work while I sleep.” Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Move to the next topic, and review the timing at the end
Write the correct timing on the client's handout for home
Note the error, and plan to reteach it at the next visit
Clarify the timing now, then ask the client to explain it again
questions.rationale:
If the client misstates information during teach-back, the nurse clarifies the confusion before moving to the next topic, then has the client explain it again. A diuretic at bedtime causes nighttime urination, broken sleep, and fall risk.

Reviewing the timing at the end isn't the right answer: the nurse does recap the whole session at the end, but leaving the error uncorrected lets it settle in and confuse later topics. Writing it on the handout doesn't confirm understanding, and waiting for the next visit sends the client home with the wrong plan.

Takeaway: When teach-back reveals an error, correct it right then and check again before going on.

questions.stem: A nurse has taught a client four topics before discharge, using teach-back after each one. Which action should the nurse take next?
options: Give the client handouts on the four topics and end the session
Ask the client to explain the main points of the whole session
Ask the client to rate his understanding on a scale of 1 to 10
Document that the teaching was completed and understood
questions.rationale:
After all the topics are taught, the nurse asks the client to explain the major points from the entire session once more. This checks that the pieces fit together and were retained.

Documenting that teaching was understood isn't the right answer: each topic was checked, but the final teach-back of the whole session hasn't been done. Handouts are a good supplement, not the final check, and a self-rating doesn't show what the client actually knows.

Takeaway: Use teach-back after each topic and again for the whole session at the end.

questions.stem: A nurse is documenting a teaching session with a client who has a new prescription for an inhaler. Which information should the nurse include?
options: The client's response to the teaching
The learning needs that were identified
The plan for further teaching
The nurse's opinion of the client's attitude
The materials given to the client
The plan used for other clients with asthma
questions.rationale:
Documentation of teaching includes the learning needs identified, the outcomes and content, the client's response and understanding, the plan for further teaching, and the resources used and given.

The nurse's opinion of the client's attitude isn't the right answer: affective learning matters, but documentation records observed behavior and the client's words, not opinions. Other clients' plans don't belong in this client's record.

Takeaway: Document needs, content, the client's response, materials given, and the plan for more teaching: facts, not opinions.

questions.stem: A nurse taught a client with heart failure about a low-sodium diet before discharge. Which finding at a home visit 1 month later best shows that the teaching was effective?
options: Her food log for recent weeks lists meals with little salt
The client scored 100% on the diet quiz given before discharge
The client says she understands why sodium matters for her heart
The client can name five common foods that are high in sodium
questions.rationale:
Evidence of learning is a change in behavior that can be observed and measured and becomes part of routine activities. A food log showing low-sodium choices every day a month later shows the behavior has become routine.

A perfect quiz score isn't the right answer: it's measurable and objective, but it shows knowledge at discharge, not changed behavior at home. Saying she understands is self-report, and naming high-sodium foods is cognitive; she could know them all and still eat them.

Takeaway: The best proof of learning is a lasting change in what the client does, not what the client knows or says.

questions.stem: A nurse is evaluating a client's use of a glucose meter after two teaching sessions. The client still can't apply the blood drop to the test strip correctly. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Refer the client to a home health agency for glucose checks
Document that the client is unable to learn this skill
Modify the teaching approach, then teach the step again
Ask a family member to take over the client's glucose checks
questions.rationale:
When evaluation shows the outcome wasn't met, the nurse modifies or repeats the teaching plan. Behavior change takes time and practice, so the nurse tries a different approach (another demonstration, a different meter, more practice) and teaches again.

Asking a family member to take over isn't the right answer: support people can help, but it gives up on a client who may learn with a different approach. Referring to home health and documenting that the client can't learn are also premature after two sessions.

Takeaway: An unmet outcome means revise and reteach; skills take time and practice.

questions.stem: A client was taught to use an inhaled controller medication twice a day. Which evaluation method gives the nurse objective data on whether the client is using it as taught at home?
options: The client's report of how often she uses the inhaler
Readings from a dose counter that records each use
A written quiz on the purpose of the controller medication
Asking the client to explain her schedule in her own words
questions.rationale:
Methods of evaluating learning include return demonstration, post-tests, oral questioning, self-report, and electronic monitoring devices. A dose counter that records each use shows what she actually does at home.

Explaining her schedule isn't the right answer: teach-back is a strong method, but it shows she knows the schedule, not that she follows it. Self-report of use is subjective, and a quiz on the medication's purpose checks knowledge only.

Takeaway: Choose the evaluation method that fits the question: knowing is checked by teach-back or tests, doing by observation or monitoring devices.

questions.stem: A nurse is about to teach a 6-year-old with asthma and her parent how to use an inhaler with a spacer. Which action should the nurse take first?
options: Direct the teaching to the parent alone
Show the steps on the child's stuffed animal
Give the parent a handout to read with the child
Assess the child's developmental level
questions.rationale:
When teaching children, the nurse first assesses the child's developmental level; it decides how the teaching is pitched and how much the child can do.

Showing the steps on a stuffed animal isn't the right answer: props are a great way to teach a child, but choosing a method before assessing the child's level skips the first step. Teaching is usually directed to the parent, but teaching only the parent leaves out the child, who should be included at her level. A handout doesn't teach the skill.

Takeaway: With children, assess developmental level first, then teach the parent and include the child at the child's level.

questions.stem: A nurse is preparing a 5-year-old for a blood draw. Which approach should the nurse use?
options: Explain the steps to the parent while the child plays nearby
Explain in detail how the lab tests the blood sample
Tell the child it won't hurt so that he stays calm
Call the child by name and show the steps on a doll
questions.rationale:
With young children, the nurse builds trust by using the child's name, uses a calm approach, and uses props to show what will happen.

Telling the child it won't hurt isn't the right answer: it aims to calm him, but it isn't true, and once it hurts the child stops trusting the nurse. Teaching only the parent leaves the child out, and a detailed explanation of lab testing is beyond a 5-year-old.

Takeaway: For young children: their name, simple honest words, props, and a calm setting.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a 15-year-old who has newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes. His mother answers every question the nurse asks him. Which approach should the nurse take?
options: Teach the mother, since she will manage his diabetes care at home
Direct the questions to the teen, and ask the mother to let him respond
Give the teen written materials to read on his own after the visit
Focus the teaching on long-term complications to stress seriousness
questions.rationale:
With adolescents, the nurse assesses their independence from parents and involves them directly; that builds the trusting relationship teaching depends on. A 15-year-old will manage much of his own care at school and with friends.

Teaching the mother isn't the right answer: parents of young children are the main learners, but a teen needs to be the learner himself. Written materials on his own skip active involvement, and long-term complications miss the teen focus: safety, consequences, and personal responsibility now.

Takeaway: Teach adolescents directly, respecting their growing independence, and focus on safety and responsibility.

questions.stem: A school nurse is planning a session on alcohol for a group of 16-year-olds. Which approach fits this age group best?
options: Present data on the long-term effects of alcohol on the liver
Invite parents to attend so they can reinforce the rules at home
Talk through ways to handle peer pressure at a party
Review the laws on the legal drinking age and their penalties
questions.rationale:
Teaching for adolescents focuses on safety, consequences, and personal responsibility, because of peer pressure and risk-taking. Practicing how to handle pressure at a party addresses the situation they will face.

Long-term liver effects isn't the right answer: it's accurate health information, but distant consequences rarely change a teen's choices tonight. Inviting parents moves the focus off the teens' own responsibility, and drinking-age laws are rules they already know.

Takeaway: With teens, make it about real situations now: peer pressure, safe choices, and their own responsibility.

questions.stem: A nurse is choosing a way to reinforce asthma teaching for a 14-year-old client. Which method is most likely to engage this client?
options: A phone app that tracks symptoms and sends reminders
A printed booklet to keep in his school backpack
A monthly group class with other parents and children
A longer talk with the provider at each clinic visit
questions.rationale:
E-health interventions, such as apps and electronic reminders, are especially helpful with adolescents, who use phones daily. An app also involves the teen actively in tracking his own care.

A monthly group class isn't the right answer: group sessions can teach many people, but a class aimed at parents and young children doesn't fit a teen's independence. A booklet is passive, and a longer talk with the provider puts the teen in the listener's role.

Takeaway: Technology-based tools fit adolescents well, and keep them active in their own care.

questions.stem: A 42-year-old who works full time is starting an anticoagulant. He says, “Just tell me what I need to do. I don't have time for a class.” Which approach should the nurse use?
options: Explain that he must attend the full anticoagulant class before he leaves
Explain briefly why each step matters, and fit the teaching to his schedule
Give him the written instructions, and let him read them when he has time
Teach just the dose and timing, since he has asked to keep it short
questions.rationale:
Adult learners need to know why they should learn something, want to be treated as self-directed, and have personal demands such as work. The nurse explains why each step matters (bleeding precautions protect him) and fits the teaching to his schedule.

Teaching only the dose and timing isn't the right answer: it respects his request, but it leaves out safety teaching he needs, like bleeding precautions. Insisting on the full class ignores his self-direction, and written instructions alone skip the explanation and any check of understanding.

Takeaway: Adults learn best when they know why it matters to them and when teaching respects their time and independence.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client with heart failure whom the nurse also taught during an admission last year. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Use the same teaching approach that worked last time
Ask the client's spouse how the client learns best
Use the approach the nurse learns best with
Reassess the client's current learning preferences
questions.rationale:
With adults, the nurse seeks the client's unique learning preferences, even if the nurse has worked with this client before. Health, stress, and needs change, so the nurse reassesses.

Using what worked last time isn't the right answer: it saves time and once fit this client, but it skips assessment. Asking the spouse goes around the client, and the nurse's own learning style may help in planning but doesn't replace the client's.

Takeaway: Reassess learning preferences each time; what worked before may not fit now.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching an 82-year-old client who has mild hearing loss about three new medications. Which approach should the nurse use?
options: Face the client, use a lower pitch, and cover one drug at a time
Face the client, raise the pitch, and cover the three drugs together
Sit at his side, use a lower pitch, and cover the three drugs together
Sit at his side, raise the pitch, and cover one drug at a time
questions.rationale:
Older adults' learning is affected by sensory changes, memory, and response time. Facing the client lets him see the nurse's face and lips; age-related hearing loss affects high pitches first, so a lower pitch is easier to hear; and covering one medication at a time allows time to process.

Sitting at his side with a lower pitch isn't the right answer: sitting down feels calm and the pitch is right, but from the side he can't see the nurse's face, and covering the three drugs together overloads memory and processing time. A raised pitch is harder to hear with age-related hearing loss, which rules out the other two choices.

Takeaway: For older adults: face them, lower your pitch, slow down, and teach one piece at a time with repetition.

questions.stem: A nurse is planning teaching for a 79-year-old client who has new chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. Which actions should the nurse include?
options: Allow extra time to process each new piece of information
Repeat the key points during and at the end of each session
Include the primary caregiver, with the client's permission
Schedule the teaching late in the day, after therapy is done
Cover the content in one longer session to save energy
Use a calm approach in a quiet, peaceful setting
questions.rationale:
With older adults, the nurse allows adequate time to process information, provides repetition, includes significant others or caregivers, and uses a calm approach in a peaceful environment.

One longer session to save energy isn't the right answer: energy level does affect learning, but a long session tires the client more and overloads memory; shorter sessions work better. Late in the day after therapy is when energy is lowest.

Takeaway: Older adults learn best with extra time, repetition, a calm quiet setting, short sessions, and their caregivers included.

questions.stem: A 78-year-old client is being discharged after a fall at home. A new blood pressure medication was started, and the client lives alone. Which teaching topic should the nurse cover first?
options: Planning low-sodium meals at home
Starting a daily walking program
Getting up slowly from a bed or chair
Scheduling the follow-up appointment
questions.rationale:
Teaching for older adults centers on nutrition, physical activity, personal safety, medications, and follow-up. A client who just fell, is starting a blood pressure medication (which can cause dizziness when standing), and lives alone is at high risk of another fall, so safety comes first: rising slowly.

Scheduling follow-up isn't the right answer: missed appointments are common and important, but it doesn't address the immediate risk of injury. Low-sodium meals and a walking program are worthwhile, but they are longer-term goals.

Takeaway: Prioritize teaching by safety: the risk that could hurt the client soonest comes first.

questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client whose primary language is Vietnamese and who speaks a little English. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the client's 12-year-old grandson to interpret
Speak slowly in simple English, and use gestures
Use a professional medical interpreter for the teaching
Give written instructions in English with pictures
questions.rationale:
Language is a cultural factor that can block learning. A professional medical interpreter makes sure the content is conveyed accurately and the client's questions are understood.

Simple English with gestures isn't the right answer: the client speaks some English, but a little everyday English isn't enough for medical teaching, and misunderstandings may go unnoticed. A child interpreter may not know medical terms and puts a child in an inappropriate role, and English handouts don't solve the language barrier.

Takeaway: When the client's primary language differs, teach through a professional medical interpreter.

questions.stem: A client tells the nurse that in her family, health decisions are made together. The nurse is planning teaching about her new medication. Which action should the nurse take?
options: Ask the client whom she would like included in the teaching
Teach the client alone, to protect the privacy of her health information
Teach the oldest family member, who usually makes the family's decisions
Teach the client first, then teach her family members in a separate session
questions.rationale:
Teaching is adjusted for the learner's culture, and the client is involved in planning. Asking whom she wants included respects her family's way of deciding while keeping her in control of her own information.

Teaching the client alone isn't the right answer: privacy matters, but she has told the nurse she wants her family involved, and the client can choose to share. Teaching the oldest member assumes who decides and bypasses the client, and separate sessions work against deciding together.

Takeaway: Let the client decide who joins the teaching, and fit the plan to the client's cultural way of making decisions.

questions.topic: Learning theories and the nurse's role
questions.stem: A nurse is teaching a client who had a stroke to feed herself with adaptive utensils. Which action by the nurse is most likely to make the client keep trying?
options: Point out each error right away so she can correct it
Hold feedback until she has finished the whole meal
Feed her once she tires, to save her energy for therapy
Praise each attempt to bring the spoon to her mouth
questions.rationale:
Behaviorist theory says a behavior is repeated when it's positively reinforced. Praise or encouragement with each attempt makes her more likely to keep trying.

Pointing out each error isn't the right answer: correction is part of feedback, but constant correction without praise discourages a struggling learner. Holding feedback until the end loses the link between the effort and the reward, and feeding her takes away the practice.

Takeaway: Reinforce each attempt with praise, and allow time to practice: rewarded behavior is repeated.

questions.topic: Learning theories and the nurse's role
questions.stem: A client with new heart failure is a retired chef who loves to cook. Which approach best builds on how this client learns?
options: Give him the standard low-sodium meal plan to follow
Have him adapt one of his own recipes to cut the sodium
Show him a video on reading sodium on food labels
Review a list of high-sodium foods he should avoid
questions.rationale:
Constructivist theory and adult learning theory both say learning builds on the learner's prior experiences. Adapting his own recipe uses his skill as a chef, and he solves the problem himself.

The standard meal plan isn't the right answer: it's accurate and complete, but it ignores his experience and gives him nothing to work out. A label video and a list of foods are useful, but they don't connect to what he already knows.

Takeaway: Build on what the learner already knows and does; problem solving with familiar material makes new learning stick.

questions.topic: Learning theories and the nurse's role
questions.stem: A client who must learn to use a peak flow meter says, “I learn best when someone shows me first.” Which sequence should the nurse use?
options: Show the steps, have him repeat them, and coach until correct
Have him try it first, then correct the steps he gets wrong
Explain each step, then give him a handout with pictures
Show the steps once, then ask him to explain them back
questions.rationale:
Social learning theory says people learn by observing and imitating a model. The nurse models the skill, then asks for repeat demonstrations until performance is satisfactory.

Showing once, then asking him to explain isn't the right answer: it uses modeling and teach-back, but explaining doesn't show he can do the skill, and one demonstration may not be enough. Trying it first reverses the order he asked for, and explaining with a handout skips the modeling.

Takeaway: Model the skill, then have the learner repeat it until it's done correctly.

questions.topic: Learning theories and the nurse's role
questions.stem: A newly licensed nurse asks why client teaching is part of every nurse's job, not only the clinical educator's. Which response by the charge nurse is accurate?
options: “It's part of the job because providers order teaching for most clients.”
“It's a courtesy we offer clients when time on the unit allows for it.”
“The ANA and The Joint Commission make it a standard of practice.”
“It's needed mainly for clients who have low health literacy skills.”
questions.rationale:
Patient education is a standard of practice for nurses, providers, and health care organizations, identified by the American Nurses Association, The Joint Commission, the American Hospital Association, and others. It's an expected part of nursing care.

Because providers order it isn't the right answer: many interventions need orders, but teaching is an independent nursing responsibility that doesn't wait for an order. It's not a courtesy when time allows, and it's not limited to clients with low literacy: every client needs teaching.

Takeaway: Client teaching is a standard of nursing practice, expected of every nurse for every client.

questions.topic: Learning theories and the nurse's role
questions.stem: A nurse has taught a client how to judge health information found online. Which statement by the client shows understanding of the teaching?
options: “A site run by the company that makes the product is most reliable.”
“I'll check who wrote it, and when it was last updated.”
“A page that many people have edited is likely to be more accurate.”
“A site with lots of positive reviews from patients can be trusted.”
questions.rationale:
To judge online health information, clients check the author's credentials (and the About Us page), citations and references, and the posting or update date.

A page many people have edited isn't the right answer: many reviewers sound like a check on errors, but popular "wiki" sites aren't quality references. Sites from companies selling the product should be viewed cautiously, and positive reviews aren't evidence.

Takeaway: Teach clients to check the author, the date, and the references, and to be cautious with sales sites and wikis.

questions.topic: Learning theories and the nurse's role
questions.stem: During teaching, a client asks the nurse about an interaction between his new medication and an herbal supplement. The nurse isn't sure of the answer. Which response should the nurse give?
options: “That's a question for your provider, so ask at your next visit.”
“Let's finish the main points first, and then come back to it.”
“I think it's fine, but I'll give you my best guess for now.”
“I'm not certain, so I'll check and get back to you before you leave.”
questions.rationale:
The art of teaching includes knowing one's own limits on a topic and encouraging the learner's questions. The nurse admits uncertainty, finds the accurate answer, and follows up before discharge.

Finishing the main points first isn't the right answer: keeping a session organized is good practice, but it puts off a safety question the nurse can't answer anyway. Referring to the next provider visit leaves a possible interaction unchecked until then, and a best guess risks giving wrong information.

Takeaway: When you don't know, say so, find the accurate answer, and follow up; never guess during teaching.

questions.topic: Learning theories and the nurse's role
questions.stem: A nurse notices growing frustration while a client asks the same question about her wound care for the third time. Which action by the nurse shows emotional intelligence?
options: Ask a coworker to take over the rest of the teaching session
Give the client a printout of the answer to reread later
Remind the client gently that the question was answered
Recognize the feeling, and answer calmly in a new way
questions.rationale:
Emotional intelligence is the ability to recognize one's own feelings and others', and to use emotions with discernment. The nurse notices her frustration, keeps it from shaping her response, and tries a new way to explain, since repeated questions often mean the first explanation didn't work.

Gently reminding the client it was answered isn't the right answer: it's polite, but it lets the nurse's frustration lead and doesn't fix the confusion. Handing off to a coworker avoids the feeling rather than managing it, and a printout repeats the same explanation.

Takeaway: Notice your own feelings, keep them out of the response, and treat a repeated question as a sign to explain differently.

questions.stem: Which findings in the nurse's notes support the client's readiness to learn the insulin pen at 1400?
options: Picks up the pen from the tray and asks to hold it
Says he wants to take care of himself at home
Says he left school in the eighth grade
Slept poorly the night before because of a roommate
Lives alone, with a daughter who visits weekly
questions.rationale:
Readiness shows as interest and engagement (he reaches for the pen and asks to hold it) and recognizing the learning need (he wants to take care of himself).

Living alone isn't the right answer: it makes the teaching more necessary, but it's a reason the learning matters, not a sign he's ready. Leaving school in eighth grade is a cue to check literacy and plan the materials, not readiness. Poor sleep lowered his readiness in the morning; it's a barrier, not support.

Takeaway: Readiness is what the client shows now (interest, questions, a stated goal); need and literacy shape the plan but don't show readiness.

questions.stem: Which plan should the nurse use to teach the client the insulin pen?
options: Teach at 0900 using a detailed written guide to each of the steps
Demonstrate at 1400, then have him practice each step with the pen
Show a video at 0900, and answer his questions about it afterward
Teach his daughter at her next visit, then have her show him the steps
questions.rationale:
Two things decide this: timing and the domain. At 0900 he was tired after a poor night; at 1400 he's rested, alert, and asking to learn. The insulin pen is a psychomotor skill, so he needs a demonstration and hands-on practice.

Teaching the daughter first isn't the right answer: family support helps, but she visits only weekly, he lives alone, and he's the one who will inject. 0900 teaching comes when fatigue blocks learning, and a detailed written guide may not suit his reading level. A video adds no practice.

Takeaway: Teach a skill when the client is rested and ready, by demonstration and practice, to the person who will do it.

questions.stem: The next morning, the nurse evaluates the insulin teaching. Which findings show the teaching plan's outcomes have been met?
options: Primes the pen with 2 units before dialing his dose
Says “I understand” after each step the nurse reviews
Explains in his own words what to do if he feels shaky and sweaty
Signs the discharge form stating insulin teaching was given
Injects into his abdomen and holds the needle for 10 seconds
Watched the full insulin pen video on the room's TV
questions.rationale:
Each outcome in the teaching plan is met by an observed behavior: he primes the pen with 2 units and injects and holds for 10 seconds (return demonstration of objectives 1 and 2), and explains in his own words what to do for low blood glucose (teach-back for objective 3).

Saying "I understand" after each step isn't the right answer: it sounds like confirmation, but agreement isn't evidence of learning. Signing the form shows teaching was given, and watching the video is exposure, not proof.

Takeaway: Evaluate each objective with a matching method: watch the skills, and have the client explain the knowledge in his own words.
